content: Non-English publications were included in the review process. Systematic evidence reviews were conducted following the methodologies outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Methods Manual. The Cochrane and AHRQ standards were adhered to for systematic searches, risk of bias assessments, and treatment effect estimations. Data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were pooled for meta-analyses when appropriate, or summarized narratively when pooling was deemed unsuitable by the systematic review team. Each systematic review team developed a detailed protocol describing their planned methods for literature searching, including databases searched, time periods covered, search strategies, trial selection, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, and data synthesis and reporting. These protocols were reviewed and edited by the WHO Technical Unit and an independent methodologist, then shared with the Guideline Development Group (GDG) for feedback before being finalized and published in an open-access repository. For each intervention, systematic review teams created structured evidence syntheses for each outcome at pre-specified time points, by comparator, and included subpopulation analyses. These were presented in a Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) evidence profile format. The GRADE system was used to assess the certainty of the evidence for a specific outcome of an intervention in a population or subpopulation. GRADE assessments were based on five criteria, which informed the determination of evidence certainty for each outcome. Certainty was graded as high, moderate, low, or very low. The GDG determined the overall certainty of evidence across all critical outcomes for each recommendation, which could differ from the systematic review team's assessment. When all outcomes pointed in the same direction (e.g., benefit or no difference), the highest certainty rating was applied overall. In cases of inconsistency in estimates and certainty ratings, the lowest certainty rating was applied. If some critical outcomes were deemed sufficient to support a recommendation, the highest certainty rating overall was selected, provided the recommendation remained unchanged even if other critical outcomes had lower certainty. The evidence and recommendations for each intervention included an evaluation of the benefits and harms of the intervention and the certainty of the evidence. The WHO guideline for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults in primary and community care settings also included a qualitative evidence synthesis focusing on older adults. This synthesis was commissioned to provide the GDG with additional insights into the values, preferences, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility of the interventions and their outcomes from the perspective of older adults and/or their caregivers. The synthesis followed the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) protocol and review template. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) approach for public health interventions. Before proposing draft recommendations, the GDG reviewed EtD summary documents for each intervention, which included GRADE evidence profile tables for each comparator and detailed subpopulation analyses. These documents also provided qualitative evidence on values, preferences, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility from the perspective of older adults and/or their caregivers. The GDG was guided in making judgments on the benefits, harms, and balance of benefits and harms for each intervention by considering the quantitative evidence and its certainty, as presented in GRADE evidence profile tables. Judgments on other EtD domains, such as values, preferences, acceptability, feasibility, equity, and human rights, were informed by GDG members' expertise, experience, and observations within their contexts. Discussions on equity and human rights focused on vulnerable populations, such as older adults, and included input from GDG members with lived experiences or expertise in gender, equity, and human rights. For the EtD domain of resource implications, the GDG considered up to three information sources, including their own knowledge and experience related to treatment costs within their settings or regions, while acknowledging variations in subsidies across health systems. Where qualitative evidence was lacking for a particular domain or intervention, judgments were based on the GDG's experience and observations. Initial draft recommendations were proposed through a consensus-driven process facilitated by an independent methodologist. Consensus was defined as a pre-specified threshold of GDG members agreeing to or being able to live with the proposed recommendation, including its direction and strength. Principles and thresholds for decision-making were established at the beginning of the second GDG meeting series. A quorum of at least two-thirds of GDG members was required to participate in any recommendation proposal, and at least 60% of members in attendance needed to agree on the proposal to formulate a recommendation. Strong recommendations were limited to cases where there was moderate or high certainty evidence supporting a balance in favor of benefits over harms (or vice versa), and/or when interventions were judged to be highly acceptable, feasible, equitable, and valued by people with chronic primary low back pain (CPLBP). Conditional recommendations were made when overall certainty was low or very low, or when judgments in other domains indicated variability or uncertainty. In some cases, no recommendation was made if the evidence was insufficient or inconclusive. Strong recommendations imply that almost all individuals with CPLBP would want the intervention, and most healthcare workers and policymakers should implement it. Conversely, strong recommendations against an intervention indicate that most individuals with CPLBP would not want the intervention, and it should not be adopted as policy in most situations. Conditional recommendations reflect uncertainty or variability in evidence or other factors, and their implementation may depend on specific contexts or individual circumstances.
